text.text: Artificial agents as leaders and followers: An integrative role-congruity review.
Group & Organization Management.
text.formatted: Group & Organization Management.

text.text: "I like robots.
I like them considerably better than I do human beings.
If a robot can be created capable of being a civil executive, I think he'd make the best one possible.
By the Laws of Robotics, he'd be incapable of harming humans, incapable of tyranny, of corruption, of stupidity, of prejudice.
Susan Calvin. Isaac Asimov, I, Robot (1950).
text.formatted: Susan Calvin. <ref type="bibr">Isaac Asimov, I, Robot (1950)</ref>.

text.text: This quote from Asimov's science-fiction short story "Evidence" (Asimov, 1950) foreshadows a phenomenon that has become increasingly salient in organizations: the emergence of robots and artificial intelligence systems as managerial actors (e.g., Tsai, Marshall, et al., 2022; Wesche & Sonderegger, 2019).
text.formatted: This quote from Asimov's science-fiction short story "Evidence" <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Asimov, 1950)</ref> foreshadows a phenomenon that has become increasingly salient in organizations: the emergence of robots and artificial intelligence systems as managerial actors (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b130">Tsai, Marshall, et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">Wesche & Sonderegger, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: On digital platforms, algorithmic systems already allocate work, monitor performance, and issue feedback (e.g., Curchod et al., 2020; Rahman, 2021).
text.formatted: On digital platforms, algorithmic systems already allocate work, monitor performance, and issue feedback (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Curchod et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">Rahman, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Recent EU-representative worker surveys show that about one in five workers is already managed by software: between 16% and 27% report that algorithmic systems allocate tasks or monitor performance (Riso et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Recent EU-representative worker surveys show that about one in five workers is already managed by software: between 16% and 27% report that algorithmic systems allocate tasks or monitor performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">(Riso et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Further, organizations are beginning to experiment with embodied forms such as virtual agents, including digital twins of executives that can attend meetings or respond to employee inquiries on their behalf (Boyle, 2025).
text.formatted: Further, organizations are beginning to experiment with embodied forms such as virtual agents, including digital twins of executives that can attend meetings or respond to employee inquiries on their behalf <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Boyle, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, hopes that algorithmic or robotic managers can deliver objective and bias-free decisions (e.g., Chamorro-Premuzic & Ahmetoglu, 2016) exist alongside perceptions that such nonhuman agents lack relevant social-emotional capacities such as empathy, care, and emotional understanding (e.g., Yam et al., 2025).
text.formatted: However, hopes that algorithmic or robotic managers can deliver objective and bias-free decisions (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Chamorro-Premuzic & Ahmetoglu, 2016)</ref> exist alongside perceptions that such nonhuman agents lack relevant social-emotional capacities such as empathy, care, and emotional understanding (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b144">Yam et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This reveals a tension between nonhuman agents occupying leader roles and the human-centric nature of leadership (Tsai, Marshall, et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This reveals a tension between nonhuman agents occupying leader roles and the human-centric nature of leadership <ref type="bibr" target="#b130">(Tsai, Marshall, et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Empirical findings mirror this tension by revealing considerable inconsistencies: Perceptions can shift depending on the ascribed organizational role.
For example, an identical chatbot labeled an "AI-based manager" was evaluated as more likable and knowledgeable than when framed as an "AI representative" (Jeon, 2022).
text.formatted: For example, an identical chatbot labeled an "AI-based manager" was evaluated as more likable and knowledgeable than when framed as an "AI representative" <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Jeon, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Adding to the complexity, perceptions also vary by design: robots high in human likeness can increase perceptions of warmth and acceptance (e.g., Wolf & Stock-Homburg, 2026), yet also be viewed as more abusive (e.g., Yam et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Adding to the complexity, perceptions also vary by design: robots high in human likeness can increase perceptions of warmth and acceptance (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b141">Wolf & Stock-Homburg, 2026</ref>), yet also be viewed as more abusive (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b145">Yam et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Some studies show that algorithmic or robotic leaders are perceived as competent, fair, or even preferable to human leaders (e.g., Höddinghaus et al., 2021; Wolf & Stock-Homburg, 2026), whereas others find that they evoke discomfort, distrust, or illegitimacy (e.g., Jago et al., 2024; McGuire & De Cremer, 2023).
text.formatted: Some studies show that algorithmic or robotic leaders are perceived as competent, fair, or even preferable to human leaders (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Höddinghaus et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b141">Wolf & Stock-Homburg, 2026)</ref>, whereas others find that they evoke discomfort, distrust, or illegitimacy (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Jago et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">McGuire & De Cremer, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This pattern of mixed reactions to the same artificial agent across roles and designs points to a common evaluative mechanism: the perceived fit, or lack of fit, between what a role is seen to require and what the agent appears to offer.

Role congruity theory (Eagly & Karau, 2002) explains this mechanism by comparing attributes that are prescribed by a professional role (e.g., what a leader should be like) and attributes that are ascribed on the basis of social categories such as gender or age (Eagly, 1987; Eagly & Wood, 2012; Koenig & Eagly, 2014).
text.formatted: Role congruity theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Eagly & Karau, 2002)</ref> explains this mechanism by comparing attributes that are prescribed by a professional role (e.g., what a leader should be like) and attributes that are ascribed on the basis of social categories such as gender or age <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Eagly, 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Eagly & Wood, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Koenig & Eagly, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: When prescribed role expectations and ascribed attributes are perceived as congruent, targets are seen as appropriate and legitimate; when they are perceived as incongruent, observers are more likely to respond with bias or resistance (del Carmen Triana et al., 2024; Eagly & Karau, 2002).
text.formatted: When prescribed role expectations and ascribed attributes are perceived as congruent, targets are seen as appropriate and legitimate; when they are perceived as incongruent, observers are more likely to respond with bias or resistance <ref type="bibr">(del Carmen Triana et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Eagly & Karau, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: As algorithmic systems and robots are perceived as social actors in organizations (e.g., Anthony et al., 2023), we extend this logic of role (in)congruity to nonhuman agents.
text.formatted: As algorithmic systems and robots are perceived as social actors in organizations (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Anthony et al., 2023)</ref>, we extend this logic of role (in)congruity to nonhuman agents.

text.text: We define these artificial agents as machine-based systems that operate with varying autonomy, adapt after deployment, and generate outputs such as predictions, recommendations, or decisions that influence physical or virtual environments (European Union, 2024).
text.formatted: We define these artificial agents as machine-based systems that operate with varying autonomy, adapt after deployment, and generate outputs such as predictions, recommendations, or decisions that influence physical or virtual environments <ref type="bibr">(European Union, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Whereas humans in organizational roles are evaluated through social categories that shape perceived role incongruity, artificial agents lack such category memberships.

Instead, we argue that observers rely on design-based social cues, such as embodiment (e.g., algorithm vs. robot) and verbal and non-verbal behavior (e.g., voice, conversational style, name), to infer an agent's attributes (e.g., Blut et al., 2021; Glikson & Woolley, 2020).
text.formatted: Instead, we argue that observers rely on design-based social cues, such as embodiment (e.g., algorithm vs. robot) and verbal and non-verbal behavior (e.g., voice, conversational style, name), to infer an agent's attributes (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Blut et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Glikson & Woolley, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: When the attributes inferred from these cues do not fit those prescribed by the role, observers perceive role incongruity, shaping how they evaluate, respond to, and adapt to artificial agents in organizational roles (del Carmen Triana et al., 2024).
text.formatted: When the attributes inferred from these cues do not fit those prescribed by the role, observers perceive role incongruity, shaping how they evaluate, respond to, and adapt to artificial agents in organizational roles <ref type="bibr">(del Carmen Triana et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This lack-of-fit mechanism clarifies why the same artificial agent may be evaluated differently across roles and designs.
Research has typically examined roles and design cues separately rather than together.

Work on artificial agents in organizations specified how these agents can occupy leader, partner, and follower roles (Tsai, Marshall, et al., 2022; Wesche & Sonderegger, 2019) and, in particular, when they can function as teammates in human-agent teams (e.g., Berretta et al., 2023; Bezrukova et al., 2023; Lyons et al., 2021; Seeber et al., 2020; Wolf & Stock-Homburg, 2023; Wynne & Lyons, 2018).
text.formatted: Work on artificial agents in organizations specified how these agents can occupy leader, partner, and follower roles <ref type="bibr" target="#b130">(Tsai, Marshall, et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">Wesche & Sonderegger, 2019)</ref> and, in particular, when they can function as teammates in human-agent teams (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Berretta et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Bezrukova et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Lyons et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b121">Seeber et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b140">Wolf & Stock-Homburg, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b142">Wynne & Lyons, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Design-focused reviews show that appearance and verbal and nonverbal behavioral cues evoke perceptions of human likeness and mind perceptions that increase perceived competence and warmth and shape acceptance (e.g., Blut et al., 2021; Liew & Tan, 2021; Wirtz et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Design-focused reviews show that appearance and verbal and nonverbal behavioral cues evoke perceptions of human likeness and mind perceptions that increase perceived competence and warmth and shape acceptance (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Blut et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Liew & Tan, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b139">Wirtz et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Trust has emerged as one focal outcome of these evaluations, and trustfocused reviews highlight performance, transparency, context, and mind perception as central antecedents of trust in artificial teammates (e.g., Benk et al., 2025; Dang & Li, 2026; Glikson & Woolley, 2020; Hancock et al., 2021; Vanneste & Puranam, 2025; Wildman et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Trust has emerged as one focal outcome of these evaluations, and trustfocused reviews highlight performance, transparency, context, and mind perception as central antecedents of trust in artificial teammates (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Benk et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Dang & Li, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Glikson & Woolley, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Hancock et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b132">Vanneste & Puranam, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b138">Wildman et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, roles and design cues have rarely been considered together, with only a few exceptions in preliminary work on machine replacement that adopt a narrower mind-role fit perspective (Dong et al., 2026; Yam et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Yet, roles and design cues have rarely been considered together, with only a few exceptions in preliminary work on machine replacement that adopt a narrower mind-role fit perspective <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Dong et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b144">Yam et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: We therefore focus on role incongruity as the underlying mechanism and combine organizational role expectations with design-based social cues to explain when and why people accept or resist artificial agents as leaders, followers, and partners.

In this integrative review, we map and explain inconsistencies in prior research on artificial agents in various organizational roles by uncovering the mechanism through which observers evaluate artificial agents as legitimate or illegitimate occupants of leader, follower, or partner roles.

To this end, we systematically review 107 empirical studies across management, psychology, engineering, and computer science, apply role incongruity as the core explanatory lens (Eagly & Karau, 2002), and later integrate the recurring patterns into a conceptual model.
text.formatted: To this end, we systematically review 107 empirical studies across management, psychology, engineering, and computer science, apply role incongruity as the core explanatory lens <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Eagly & Karau, 2002)</ref>, and later integrate the recurring patterns into a conceptual model.

text.text: When prescribed role expectations and ascribed attributes are perceived as congruent, artificial agents are judged as legitimate role occupants; when they are perceived as incongruent, illegitimacy perceptions dominate.

We further organize the breadth of indicators used in (in)congruity evaluations into two fundamental dimensions of social perception: a task dimension capturing competence and assertiveness and a social-emotional dimension comprising warmth and morality (Abele et al., 2021).
text.formatted: We further organize the breadth of indicators used in (in)congruity evaluations into two fundamental dimensions of social perception: a task dimension capturing competence and assertiveness and a social-emotional dimension comprising warmth and morality <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abele et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: We focus on these dimensions because they summarize the criteria by which leader and follower roles are evaluated (e.g., Benson et al., 2024; Nichols et al., 2026).

text.text: Following a human-centric perspective on emerging technologies (e.g., Parker et al., 2026), we place observers' perceptions at the center of the analysis: Whether an artificial agent can function in an organizational role depends both on its capabilities and on the people who work with it.
text.formatted: Following a human-centric perspective on emerging technologies (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">Parker et al., 2026)</ref>, we place observers' perceptions at the center of the analysis: Whether an artificial agent can function in an organizational role depends both on its capabilities and on the people who work with it.

text.text: With our review, we contribute to this understanding in three ways.

First, we organize and integrate a large and fragmented body of evidence spanning management, psychology, engineering, and computer science, and show that a role-incongruity lens extracts coherent patterns from findings that had appeared inconsistent: competent-yet-cold evaluations of agent leaders, relative congruity for agent followers, and conditional acceptance of agent partners and teammates.

Second, weaving in the recurring patterns identified in our review, we extend role congruity theory to artificial agents through the Artificial Agent Role Congruity (AARC) model, explaining how these differing evaluations emerge from the fit or misfit between attributes inferred from design-based cues and attributes prescribed for organizational roles.
This clarifies that established role mechanisms apply when the role occupant is nonhuman, answering calls to ground human-AI research in established psychological theory (Bigman et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This clarifies that established role mechanisms apply when the role occupant is nonhuman, answering calls to ground human-AI research in established psychological theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Bigman et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Third, we set an AARC-based agenda for future research on role-design fit, spanning theoretical, methodological, and practical questions.

In this integrative review, we combine role congruity theory (del Carmen Triana et al., 2024; Eagly & Karau, 2002) with research on human-robot and human-agent collaboration (e.g., Tsai, Marshall, et al., 2022; Yam et al., 2025) into an evaluative lens for how observers perceive artificial agents in organizational roles.
text.formatted: In this integrative review, we combine role congruity theory <ref type="bibr">(del Carmen Triana et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Eagly & Karau, 2002)</ref> with research on human-robot and human-agent collaboration (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b130">Tsai, Marshall, et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b144">Yam et al., 2025)</ref> into an evaluative lens for how observers perceive artificial agents in organizational roles.

text.text: We organize our review around three elements: (1) organizational roles as prescriptive expectations (leader, follower, partner), (2) design-based features as social cues from which observers ascribe attributes, and (3) the comparison between prescribed role expectations and ascribed attributes underlying perceived role (in)congruity.
Within organizations, actors occupy roles that carry distinct functions and expectations.
Role theory conceptualizes these expectations as socially shared sets of norms that define appropriate attributes and behavior for occupants of specific positions (Anglin et al., 2022; Biddle, 1986).
text.formatted: Role theory conceptualizes these expectations as socially shared sets of norms that define appropriate attributes and behavior for occupants of specific positions <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Anglin et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Biddle, 1986)</ref>.

text.text: As a consequence, roles provide a reference for evaluation; observers compare what the organizational role prescribes with how they perceive a target.

Role congruity theory (Eagly & Karau, 2002) formalizes this evaluative mechanism as a comparison between two sets of expectations: the attributes prescribed by a functional role, such as a leader or follower role, and the attributes ascribed to a target based on a salient social category (e.g., gender; Eagly & Wood, 2012; Koenig & Eagly, 2014).
text.formatted: Role congruity theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Eagly & Karau, 2002)</ref> formalizes this evaluative mechanism as a comparison between two sets of expectations: the attributes prescribed by a functional role, such as a leader or follower role, and the attributes ascribed to a target based on a salient social category (e.g., gender; <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Eagly & Wood, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Koenig & Eagly, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: When these attributes are incongruent, observers perceive or anticipate a lack of fit and respond with bias or resistance (Eagly & Karau, 2002; Heilman, 1983).
text.formatted: When these attributes are incongruent, observers perceive or anticipate a lack of fit and respond with bias or resistance <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Eagly & Karau, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Heilman, 1983)</ref>.

text.text: For example, when leader roles emphasize assertiveness and authority, individuals who are instead stereotyped as more communal and less agentic may be evaluated as less congruent with these roles (Koenig et al., 2011).
text.formatted: For example, when leader roles emphasize assertiveness and authority, individuals who are instead stereotyped as more communal and less agentic may be evaluated as less congruent with these roles <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Koenig et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: We organize perceived (in)congruity around two fundamental dimensions of social perception: a task dimension capturing competence and assertiveness, and a social-emotional dimension capturing warmth and morality (Abele et al., 2016 (Abele et al., , 2021)).
text.formatted: We organize perceived (in)congruity around two fundamental dimensions of social perception: a task dimension capturing competence and assertiveness, and a social-emotional dimension capturing warmth and morality <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Abele et al., 2016</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abele et al., , 2021))</ref>.

text.text: Competence and assertiveness both concern accomplishing work and exerting influence, whereas warmth and morality both concern relating to others, and they relate more strongly within than between the two dimensions (Koch et al., 2024; Yzerbyt et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Competence and assertiveness both concern accomplishing work and exerting influence, whereas warmth and morality both concern relating to others, and they relate more strongly within than between the two dimensions <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Koch et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Yzerbyt et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Observers perceive a target along these dimensions and compare this perception with what the role prescribes; (in)congruity is the fit or misfit between the two.
Further, management research distinguishes three classes of role-incongruity effects: target evaluations, target outcomes, and target adaptation (del Carmen Triana et al., 2024).

text.text: For instance, role incongruity can emerge when organizational role expectations conflict with attributes associated with race (e.g., Paluch & Shum, 2024; Sy et al., 2010), age (Daldrop et al., 2025; Diekman & Hirnisey, 2007), or sexual orientation (Liberman & Golom, 2015; Rule et al., 2016).

text.text: We extend this theory to explain how people judge artificial agents in organizational roles.

While role congruity theory traditionally focuses on human social categories, artificial agents have become salient social actors in organizations (Anthony et al., 2023; Harris-Watson & Larson, 2026).
text.formatted: While role congruity theory traditionally focuses on human social categories, artificial agents have become salient social actors in organizations <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Anthony et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Harris-Watson & Larson, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This continues the "computers are social actors" (CASA) paradigm, which showed that people apply human social rules and expectations to computers and other artificial agents (Nass et al., 1994 (Nass et al., , 1996)).
text.formatted: This continues the "computers are social actors" (CASA) paradigm, which showed that people apply human social rules and expectations to computers and other artificial agents <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">(Nass et al., 1994</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">(Nass et al., , 1996))</ref>.

text.text: People hold mental models about robotic and algorithmic agents (Banks, 2020; Cena & Grasso, 2026) and apply social perceptions to them (Nass & Moon, 2000).
text.formatted: People hold mental models about robotic and algorithmic agents <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Banks, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Cena & Grasso, 2026)</ref> and apply social perceptions to them <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">(Nass & Moon, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Because they evaluate these agents along the same dimensions that guide human judgments, such as competence and warmth (e.g., Harris-Watson et al., 2023; McKee et al., 2024), artificial agents can be perceived as congruent or incongruent with their organizational roles, much as human role occupants are.
text.formatted: Because they evaluate these agents along the same dimensions that guide human judgments, such as competence and warmth (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Harris-Watson et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">McKee et al., 2024)</ref>, artificial agents can be perceived as congruent or incongruent with their organizational roles, much as human role occupants are.

text.text: Artificial agents increasingly occupy a range of organizational roles, including follower, partner, and even leader roles (e.g., Tsai, Marshall, et al., 2022; Wesche & Sonderegger, 2019).
text.formatted: Artificial agents increasingly occupy a range of organizational roles, including follower, partner, and even leader roles (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b130">Tsai, Marshall, et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">Wesche & Sonderegger, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Whether an agent is perceived as congruent or incongruent therefore depends on what its role prescribes, which we turn to next.
Organizational roles function as shared cognitive schemas that define expectations for behavior and abilities within hierarchical and collaborative structures (Anglin et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Organizational roles function as shared cognitive schemas that define expectations for behavior and abilities within hierarchical and collaborative structures <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Anglin et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Research on implicit leadership and followership theories demonstrates that people hold mental models of leaders and followers: sets of attributes and behaviors that describe ideal members of each category (Lord et al., 1984 (Lord et al., , 2020)).
text.formatted: Research on implicit leadership and followership theories demonstrates that people hold mental models of leaders and followers: sets of attributes and behaviors that describe ideal members of each category <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">(Lord et al., 1984</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">(Lord et al., , 2020))</ref>.

text.text: Leaders are expected to provide direction, coordination, and influence and to score high on both the task and the social-emotional dimension (Junker & van Dick, 2014).
text.formatted: Leaders are expected to provide direction, coordination, and influence and to score high on both the task and the social-emotional dimension <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Junker & van Dick, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: On the task dimension, leaders should be competent, able to analyze, decide, and execute effectively, and appropriately assertive; assertiveness is seen as ideal when it guides and coordinates action but counter-ideal when expressed as dominance (Benson et al., 2024; Offermann & Coats, 2018).
text.formatted: On the task dimension, leaders should be competent, able to analyze, decide, and execute effectively, and appropriately assertive; assertiveness is seen as ideal when it guides and coordinates action but counter-ideal when expressed as dominance <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Benson et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">Offermann & Coats, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: On the social-emotional dimension, leaders are expected to show moral integrity, that is, fairness, honesty, and responsibility for others' welfare, alongside warmth (Den Hartog et al., 1999; Offermann & Coats, 2018).
text.formatted: On the social-emotional dimension, leaders are expected to show moral integrity, that is, fairness, honesty, and responsibility for others' welfare, alongside warmth (Den <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Hartog et al., 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">Offermann & Coats, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: These social-emotional qualities are central to ideal-leader expectations and can even take precedence over assertiveness in followers' preferences (Daldrop et al., 2025; Ponce de Leon & Bailey, 2025).
text.formatted: These social-emotional qualities are central to ideal-leader expectations and can even take precedence over assertiveness in followers' preferences <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Daldrop et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">Ponce de Leon & Bailey, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Followers are expected to be dependable, conscientious, and loyal, carrying out directives and supporting collective goals (Junker et al., 2016; Sy, 2010).
text.formatted: Followers are expected to be dependable, conscientious, and loyal, carrying out directives and supporting collective goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Junker et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b126">Sy, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: On the task dimension, expectations are modest: followers need enough competence to perform reliably, while assertiveness is expected to stay low, since dominance or overt self-promotion contradicts the deferential nature of followership (Bastardoz & Van Vugt, 2019; Benson et al., 2024).
text.formatted: On the task dimension, expectations are modest: followers need enough competence to perform reliably, while assertiveness is expected to stay low, since dominance or overt self-promotion contradicts the deferential nature of followership <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Bastardoz & Van Vugt, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Benson et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: On the social-emotional dimension, the central expectations are warmth and supportive engagement, centered on cooperation rather than the moral authority expected of leaders (Benson et al., 2024; Junker et al., 2016).
text.formatted: On the social-emotional dimension, the central expectations are warmth and supportive engagement, centered on cooperation rather than the moral authority expected of leaders <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Benson et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Junker et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: People also hold expectations of partners, including teammates and colleagues, who collaborate as equals rather than within a hierarchy of authority.

On the task dimension, expectations are moderate: partners should be competent enough to contribute reliably and to coordinate and communicate with others, but without the directive authority expected of leaders (Stevens & Campion, 1994).
text.formatted: On the task dimension, expectations are moderate: partners should be competent enough to contribute reliably and to coordinate and communicate with others, but without the directive authority expected of leaders <ref type="bibr" target="#b125">(Stevens & Campion, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: On the social-emotional dimension, warmth carries particular weight among equals rather than the deference expected of followers; people favor warm, cooperative colleagues and, when choosing whom to work with, interpersonal liking can even outweigh competence (Casciaro & Lobo, 2008).
text.formatted: On the social-emotional dimension, warmth carries particular weight among equals rather than the deference expected of followers; people favor warm, cooperative colleagues and, when choosing whom to work with, interpersonal liking can even outweigh competence <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Casciaro & Lobo, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: We have outlined what observers expect of leaders, followers, and partners.
But how do people assess the fit between an artificial agent and the expectations of these roles?
We argue that observers rely on the artificial agent's design-based social cues to ascribe attributes that make it appear congruent or incongruent with leader, follower, or partner roles.
Design-based social cues are the appearance and behavioral features designed into an artificial agent that signal its social presence to observers (Blut et al., 2021; Liew & Tan, 2021).
text.formatted: Design-based social cues are the appearance and behavioral features designed into an artificial agent that signal its social presence to observers <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Blut et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Liew & Tan, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: These cues fall into two broad categories: appearance and verbal and non-verbal behavior.

Appearance cues capture embodiment, an agent's form, degree of human likeness, and movement quality, ranging from disembodied algorithmic systems and voice-based assistants to virtual avatars and physically embodied robots (Glikson & Woolley, 2020; Liew & Tan, 2021).
text.formatted: Appearance cues capture embodiment, an agent's form, degree of human likeness, and movement quality, ranging from disembodied algorithmic systems and voice-based assistants to virtual avatars and physically embodied robots <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Glikson & Woolley, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Liew & Tan, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Verbal and non-verbal behavioral cues include communicative features such as voice, language style, responsiveness and turn-taking, gaze, gesture, facial expression, and labeling (Blut et al., 2021; Liew & Tan, 2021).
text.formatted: Verbal and non-verbal behavioral cues include communicative features such as voice, language style, responsiveness and turn-taking, gaze, gesture, facial expression, and labeling <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Blut et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Liew & Tan, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Such communicative cues, for example polite or empathic phrasing, increase perceived social presence and human likeness (Banks et al., 2023; Jeon, 2022).
text.formatted: Such communicative cues, for example polite or empathic phrasing, increase perceived social presence and human likeness <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Banks et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Jeon, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Design-based social cues, particularly those conveying social presence and human likeness, may enable people to infer specific attributes of the agent (Epley et al., 2007; Liew & Tan, 2021).
text.formatted: Design-based social cues, particularly those conveying social presence and human likeness, may enable people to infer specific attributes of the agent <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Epley et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Liew & Tan, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: One potential route from social cues to ascribed attributes runs through mind perception: observers infer the extent of the agent's mind along two capacities, agency (i.e., the capacity for self-control and planning) and experience (i.e., the capacity to feel and sense; Gray et al., 2007; Waytz et al., 2010).

text.text: These two capacities map loosely onto the same task and socialemotional dimensions that structure role expectations (e.g., Au & Ng, 2021).

text.text: On the task dimension, perceived agency corresponds most clearly with competence and assertiveness.

On the social-emotional dimension of role attributions, perceived experience corresponds with warmth, whereas both perceived agency and perceived experience map onto morality, the second facet of the social-emotional dimension (Gray et al., 2012).

text.text: Recent research increasingly uses mind perception to explain how people relate to artificial agents at work: as a framework for human-agent teams (Harris-Watson & Larson, 2026), as a driver of how employees craft their relationships with industrial robots (Goštautaitė et al., 2026), and as an account of threat and fear of replacement across professional roles, such as doctors and judges, and personal ones, such as companions (Dong et al., 2026; Yam et al., 2025).

text.text: This synthesis informed the coding scheme of our review (see Method).
To answer our research question, we conducted a systematic review of the empirical literature on how people evaluate artificial agents in organizational roles.
The Online Supplement, coding materials, and complete coded dataset are available on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/582jn/ overview).
text.formatted: The Online Supplement, coding materials, and complete coded dataset are available on the Open Science Framework (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/582jn/">https://osf.io/582jn/</ref> overview).

text.text: We searched PsycINFO, Business Source Premier, and IEEE Xplore in June 2025, combining artificial-agent terms with social-perception constructs, and supplemented the database results with backward and forward citation tracing and targeted journal searches (full search string and per-source counts in Section A of the Online Supplement).

We included peer-reviewed empirical studies with human participants that examined an artificial agent (i.e., robot, AI system, avatar, or algorithm) in an organizational or task context and reported at least one perception of, or evaluative or acceptance response to, the agent in a leader, follower, or partner role.
We restricted the review to studies that frame artificial agents as occupants of organizational roles, where role prescriptions are at stake.

We excluded purely technical or conceptual papers, consumer-only studies without a work or team setting, and studies whose measured outcomes concerned only the human worker, third parties, or a nonagent object (full criteria in Section A of the Online Supplement).

Screening followed PRISMA guidelines (Page et al., 2021): after deduplication, records were screened at title, abstract, and full text against these criteria, manually, with uncertain cases resolved by the author team and no automated tools used to exclude records.

text.text: For each study we coded the agent's assigned role, that is, leader, follower, partner, or team member (Tsai, Marshall, et al., 2022); its design-based cues, both appearance and verbal and non-verbal behavior (Blut et al., 2021; Glikson & Woolley, 2020); the evaluation on the task (competence, assertiveness) and social-emotional (warmth, morality) dimensions (Abele et al., 2021); responses to role (in)congruity; and contextual variables (domain, research design, and sample region).

text.text: The full coding documentation, including the codebook and scheme development, is provided in the Online Supplement (Sections B and C), and descriptive characteristics of the included studies are reported in Section D.
We reviewed 107 empirical studies to identify evaluations indicating role congruity or role incongruity.
Guided by role congruity theory (Eagly & Karau, 2002), we identified role incongruity when evaluations are inconsistent with the attributes a role is expected to require.
text.formatted: Guided by role congruity theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Eagly & Karau, 2002)</ref>, we identified role incongruity when evaluations are inconsistent with the attributes a role is expected to require.

text.text: We classified evaluations as incongruent when studies report lower evaluations on role-central facets (e.g., lower competence or morality for leaders; lower reliability-linked competence for followers; lower warmth or morality for partners) or evaluations that signal a violation of role expectations (e.g., excessive assertiveness for followers).
In contrast, we classified evaluations as congruent when they indicate alignment with role-central facets and do not show evidence of role violations.
Using this rule set, we examine how an agent's assigned role and its design-based social cues relate to evaluations, and we summarize recurring patterns of congruity and incongruity by role.

Summary tables present representative studies for agents as leaders (Table A1), followers (Table A2), and partners or teammates (Table A3); the full coded dataset is available on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/582jn/).

text.text: The review reveals a recent acceleration in research on perceptions of artificial agents in organizational or task-related roles, with 89% of studies published in 2020 or later (95 of 107).

Work prior to 2015 primarily consisted of social robotics and trust experiments (e.g., Salem et al., 2013), while the period from 2016 to 2019 marked the first integration of workplace-relevant contexts linking human likeness to evaluations of competence and warmth (Castro-González et al., 2016; Lee, 2018).
text.formatted: Work prior to 2015 primarily consisted of social robotics and trust experiments (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b118">Salem et al., 2013)</ref>, while the period from 2016 to 2019 marked the first integration of workplace-relevant contexts linking human likeness to evaluations of competence and warmth <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Castro-González et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Lee, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Research starting in 2020 increasingly addressed algorithmic and robotic leadership (e.g., Jago et al., 2024; McGuire & De Cremer, 2023), teamwork and collaboration (e.g., Fraune et al., 2020; Harris-Watson et al., 2023), and service or caregiving settings (e.g., Paluch et al., 2022; Yam et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Research starting in 2020 increasingly addressed algorithmic and robotic leadership (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Jago et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">McGuire & De Cremer, 2023)</ref>, teamwork and collaboration (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Fraune et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Harris-Watson et al., 2023)</ref>, and service or caregiving settings (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">Paluch et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b143">Yam et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Across disciplines, leader-role research is concentrated in management and psychology, partner-and teammate-role research in robotics, engineering, and computer science, and follower-role research is spread more evenly across fields.
Detailed distributions by publication year, disciplinary field, primary context, agent design type, research design, and sample region are provided in the Online Supplement Section D (Tables S5-S11).

text.text: A recurring pattern emerges for artificial agents in leader roles: they are often credited with task competence but fall short on the warmth, benevolence, and legitimacy that leadership also requires.
On the task dimension, artificial leaders are frequently judged competent.

An AI avatar delivering a vision was rated more competent, though less warm, than a human delivering the same vision (Buss et al., 2025); robotic managers are accepted more readily on performancerelated than on relational aspects (Wolf & Stock-Homburg, 2026).
text.formatted: An AI avatar delivering a vision was rated more competent, though less warm, than a human delivering the same vision <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Buss et al., 2025)</ref>; robotic managers are accepted more readily on performancerelated than on relational aspects <ref type="bibr" target="#b141">(Wolf & Stock-Homburg, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Automated leaders can also be seen as comparable in ability and higher in consistency and transparency than human leaders (Höddinghaus et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Automated leaders can also be seen as comparable in ability and higher in consistency and transparency than human leaders <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Höddinghaus et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The consistent deficit is on the social-emotional dimension.

Artificial leaders and their decisions are perceived as less fair, trustworthy, and benevolent than human counterparts (Li & Bitterly, 2024; McGuire & De Cremer, 2023; Wesche et al., 2024), particularly for decisions seen to require human judgment (Lee, 2018).
text.formatted: Artificial leaders and their decisions are perceived as less fair, trustworthy, and benevolent than human counterparts <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">(Li & Bitterly, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">McGuire & De Cremer, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b135">Wesche et al., 2024)</ref>, particularly for decisions seen to require human judgment <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">(Lee, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Anthropomorphic and agentic design cues do not reliably close this gap and can even widen it: humanlike robot supervisors elicit greater perceived agency and, in turn, perceptions of abuse and supervisor-directed retaliation when delivering negative feedback (Yam et al., 2022), and employees comply less with unethical instructions from AI than from human supervisors (Lanz et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Anthropomorphic and agentic design cues do not reliably close this gap and can even widen it: humanlike robot supervisors elicit greater perceived agency and, in turn, perceptions of abuse and supervisor-directed retaliation when delivering negative feedback <ref type="bibr" target="#b145">(Yam et al., 2022)</ref>, and employees comply less with unethical instructions from AI than from human supervisors <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(Lanz et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, the evidence points to a competent-but-cold pattern: artificial leaders can meet competence expectations yet fall short on the benevolence, fairness, and legitimacy that confer standing in leader roles, an incongruity concentrated on the social-emotional dimension.

text.text: For artificial agents in follower or subordinate roles (e.g., service, assistive, or support functions), the evidence points to congruity between design-based cues and follower-role expectations.
When design features signal social responsiveness without asserting authority, agents are generally evaluated as both warm and competent (Yang et al., 2025).
text.formatted: When design features signal social responsiveness without asserting authority, agents are generally evaluated as both warm and competent <ref type="bibr" target="#b146">(Yang et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Anthropomorphic cues that convey emotional capacity raise perceived experience and satisfaction (Yam et al., 2021) and foster relational investment, including parasocial bonds with the agent (Noor et al., 2022), while warm, attentive service agents enhance psychological ownership and revisit intentions (Ruiz-Equihua et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Anthropomorphic cues that convey emotional capacity raise perceived experience and satisfaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b143">(Yam et al., 2021)</ref> and foster relational investment, including parasocial bonds with the agent <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">(Noor et al., 2022)</ref>, while warm, attentive service agents enhance psychological ownership and revisit intentions <ref type="bibr" target="#b116">(Ruiz-Equihua et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Functional cues that signal reliability and capability, in turn, build the competence-based trust that drives adoption (Kraus et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Functional cues that signal reliability and capability, in turn, build the competence-based trust that drives adoption <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Kraus et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The pattern reverses mainly when human-likeness becomes too pronounced: a highly anthropomorphic, physically present driving agent lowered perceived control and cognitive trust relative to a virtual one (Cheng et al., 2022).
text.formatted: The pattern reverses mainly when human-likeness becomes too pronounced: a highly anthropomorphic, physically present driving agent lowered perceived control and cognitive trust relative to a virtual one <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Cheng et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: On balance, the follower evidence supports role congruity, with most design-based cues aligning with follower-role expectations for warmth, responsiveness, and dependable performance.

This evidence base is concentrated in service and caregiving contexts (23 of 37 follower studies, 62%; 18 retail or service and 5 healthcare) and includes only two internal-office studies, so we see the congruity pattern as most directly applicable to service and caregiving settings.
We present sample studies for agents as followers in Table A2.
text.formatted: We present sample studies for agents as followers in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">A2</ref>.

text.text: For artificial agents positioned as partners or team members, evaluations are mixed and depend on boundary conditions.

Agents that signal prosocial orientation and competence are generally accepted: prosocial (high social-value-orientation) agents are rated warmer, and warmth drives partner preference and continued cooperation beyond objective performance (McKee et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Agents that signal prosocial orientation and competence are generally accepted: prosocial (high social-value-orientation) agents are rated warmer, and warmth drives partner preference and continued cooperation beyond objective performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">(McKee et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: A more humanlike agent framed as a teammate also elicits greater initial trust and willingness to collaborate (Mirowska & Arsenyan, 2025).
text.formatted: A more humanlike agent framed as a teammate also elicits greater initial trust and willingness to collaborate <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">(Mirowska & Arsenyan, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Acceptance erodes when an agent falls short of the expectations its framing creates.

A "colleague" framing raises expectations that an error-prone agent fails to meet, creating frustration (Einola et al., 2024); moral violations reduce trust more sharply than equally consequential performance failures (Rezaei Khavas et al., 2024); and strongly anthropomorphic collaborative robots raise perceived intelligence and, in turn, perceived threat and negative attitudes (Liao et al., 2024).
text.formatted: A "colleague" framing raises expectations that an error-prone agent fails to meet, creating frustration <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Einola et al., 2024)</ref>; moral violations reduce trust more sharply than equally consequential performance failures <ref type="bibr" target="#b111">(Rezaei Khavas et al., 2024)</ref>; and strongly anthropomorphic collaborative robots raise perceived intelligence and, in turn, perceived threat and negative attitudes <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">(Liao et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Team composition matters as well: interpersonal trust and identification are lower in two-member human-AI dyads than in all-human dyads, though this pattern was attenuated in three-member teams (Georganta & Ulfert, 2024).
text.formatted: Team composition matters as well: interpersonal trust and identification are lower in two-member human-AI dyads than in all-human dyads, though this pattern was attenuated in three-member teams <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Georganta & Ulfert, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Collectively, these findings tie evaluations of partner and teammate agents to the interaction between role prescriptions for reciprocity and cooperation and the attributes inferred from design cues.

Role congruity emerges when cues signal enough social presence and experience to support trust and coordination without so much agency or autonomy that they violate relational expectations; role incongruity emerges when anthropomorphic or agentic cues exceed those expectations, eliciting discomfort or threat.

text.text: We develop the Artificial Agent Role Congruity (AARC) model by extending role congruity theory (Eagly & Karau, 2002) to artificial agents.
text.formatted: We develop the Artificial Agent Role Congruity (AARC) model by extending role congruity theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Eagly & Karau, 2002)</ref> to artificial agents.

text.text: AARC formalizes how observers compare prescribed expectations of organizational roles with ascribed attributes inferred from an artificial agent's design (Figure 2), producing perceptions of role congruity or role incongruity.
text.formatted: AARC formalizes how observers compare prescribed expectations of organizational roles with ascribed attributes inferred from an artificial agent's design (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2</ref>), producing perceptions of role congruity or role incongruity.

text.text: We present AARC as a conceptual model (Rousseau, 2026) that invites empirical testing and refinement.
text.formatted: We present AARC as a conceptual model <ref type="bibr" target="#b113">(Rousseau, 2026)</ref> that invites empirical testing and refinement.

text.text: The model organizes the evidence reviewed above and identifies when, how, and why artificial agents are evaluated differently across organizational roles.
Note.
The AARC model illustrates how role-based expectations and design-based social cues shape evaluations of artificial agents.
Two sets of expectations, the prescriptions of the organizational role and the artificial-agent schema, are compared with the attributes ascribed to the agent.
Design-based social cues are read, through mind perception (agency and experience), as ascribed attributes along two dimensions of social perception.

Perceived role (in)congruity is the fit or misfit between these ascribed attributes and what the role and schema prescribe, which in turn shapes evaluative outcomes and adaptations such as acceptance, trust, and legitimacy.
As our review through a role incongruity lens suggests, the combination of roles and design features determines how artificial agents are evaluated.
Whereas role congruity is attained when role and design match, two types of role incongruity are conceivable.
In roles > design configurations, the expectations attached to functional or organizational roles exceed what the agent's design appears to offer.
text.formatted: In roles > design configurations, the expectations attached to functional or organizational roles exceed what the agent's design appears to offer.

text.text: Agents framed as leaders, colleagues, or partners are expected to display empathy and moral intent, yet their design typically signals limited social presence or experience.

This shortcoming may generate a deficit on the social-emotional dimension, leading observers to perceive them as tools or morally inadequate actors (Einola & Khoreva, 2023; McGuire & De Cremer, 2023).
text.formatted: This shortcoming may generate a deficit on the social-emotional dimension, leading observers to perceive them as tools or morally inadequate actors <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Einola & Khoreva, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">McGuire & De Cremer, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, design > roles configurations occur when an agent's design implies more agency, dominance, or human likeness than its role requires.
text.formatted: In contrast, design > roles configurations occur when an agent's design implies more agency, dominance, or human likeness than its role requires.

text.text: For example, anthropomorphic or socially assertive cobots may appear overly competent or intrusive in subordinate or tool roles, causing threat or unease (Liao et al., 2023 (Liao et al., , 2024;; Stanton & Stevens, 2017).
text.formatted: For example, anthropomorphic or socially assertive cobots may appear overly competent or intrusive in subordinate or tool roles, causing threat or unease <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(Liao et al., 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">(Liao et al., , 2024;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">Stanton & Stevens, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Both patterns reduce congruity between role-based prescriptions and design-based social cues, thereby defining the core antecedent of role incongruity in line with the AARC model.
Taken together, the AARC model adds three elements beyond role congruity theory applied to a new class of role occupants.
First, in artificial agent evaluation design-based social cues replace social-category cues as the source of ascribed attributes.

What gender, age, or social class signal for role congruity evaluations in research on human role occupants, embodiment, voice, language, and labeling signal for artificial agents; because designers can control these cues, ascribed attributes become a design parameter rather than a demographic given.

Second, mind perception bridges cues and evaluation: perceived agency feeds the task dimension and perceived experience the social-emotional dimension, so the model predicts that experience cues carry more evaluative weight in roles whose prescriptions emphasize warmth and morality.
Third, the artificial agent schema-that is, the shared expectations about how robots or algorithms should act and relate (e.g., reliability, precision, obedience, neutrality, cooperation;
Banks, 2020)-constitutes a second layer of (in)congruity, so an agent can satisfy its organizational role prescriptions yet violate this artificial agent schema.
Together, these elements specify the extent of perceived misfit and why it emerges, rather than merely noting that artificial agents differ from human role occupants.
With this review, we asked how role-based expectations and design-based inferences jointly shape evaluations of artificial agents in organizational contexts.
Three patterns emerged.
First, artificial agents in leader roles often face role incongruity, particularly on the socialemotional dimension.
Second, agents in follower roles generally elicit congruity, especially in service and caregiving settings.
Third, congruity in partner roles depends on design and context.

These patterns represent the AARC model's mechanism: role prescriptions and the attributes inferred from design jointly shape evaluations on the task (competence, assertiveness) and social-emotional (warmth, morality) dimensions (Abele et al., 2021).
text.formatted: These patterns represent the AARC model's mechanism: role prescriptions and the attributes inferred from design jointly shape evaluations on the task (competence, assertiveness) and social-emotional (warmth, morality) dimensions <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abele et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Across roles, incongruity took two forms: either role demands exceeded what the design conveyed (roles > design), or the design implied more agency or human likeness than the role required (design > roles).
text.formatted: Across roles, incongruity took two forms: either role demands exceeded what the design conveyed (roles > design), or the design implied more agency or human likeness than the role required (design > roles).

text.text: Notably, humanlike design rarely repairs the leader-role deficit; if anything, greater human likeness intensifies discomfort by amplifying perceived agency without a matching gain in perceived moral understanding, consistent with accounts of AI trust as resting jointly on morality and performance (Everett et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Notably, humanlike design rarely repairs the leader-role deficit; if anything, greater human likeness intensifies discomfort by amplifying perceived agency without a matching gain in perceived moral understanding, consistent with accounts of AI trust as resting jointly on morality and performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Everett et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Our review suggests three theoretical extensions.
The first links the model to the mindperception account of machine replacement.

That literature frames reactions to machines as a matter of mind-role fit, the correspondence between the mind ascribed to an agent and the mind a role is taken to require (Dong et al., 2026; Yam et al., 2025).
text.formatted: That literature frames reactions to machines as a matter of mind-role fit, the correspondence between the mind ascribed to an agent and the mind a role is taken to require <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Dong et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b144">Yam et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In role-congruity terms, this is a lack of fit between prescribed and ascribed attributes in which the ascribed attributes are the agent's perceived mind; mind-role (mis)fit is therefore a special case of role (in)congruity rather than a separate mechanism.
Because perceived mind comprises two capacities, agency and experience, the dimension on which the lack of fit appears is predictable.

In leader roles, incongruity arises when design cues convey agency but little experience, so that agents are judged competent yet lacking in warmth and moral intent (e.g., McGuire & De Cremer, 2023; Rubin et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In leader roles, incongruity arises when design cues convey agency but little experience, so that agents are judged competent yet lacking in warmth and moral intent (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">McGuire & De Cremer, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">Rubin et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In follower roles, the lack of fit reverses, as mind-like cues exceed what a controllable, impersonal role prescribes (e.g., Appel et al., 2020).
text.formatted: In follower roles, the lack of fit reverses, as mind-like cues exceed what a controllable, impersonal role prescribes (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Appel et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In partner and teammate roles, a comparable surplus of agency or deficit of experience conflicts with the reciprocity and warmth these roles prescribe (e.g., Banks et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In partner and teammate roles, a comparable surplus of agency or deficit of experience conflicts with the reciprocity and warmth these roles prescribe (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Banks et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Framed this way, the mind-perception account of machine replacement is subsumed within the broader role-congruity logic of the AARC model.
Within our AARC model, an agent's design not only constitutes a set of cues but can also serve as a baseline "artificial agent role" schema.

When an agent's behavior or perceived attributes violate this artificial agent schema, observers may perceive a role violation that is comparable to violating a social role such as the gender role in role congruity theory, where prejudice can arise from failing to meet the prescriptions of a social role over and above the functional role itself (Eagly & Karau, 2002).
text.formatted: When an agent's behavior or perceived attributes violate this artificial agent schema, observers may perceive a role violation that is comparable to violating a social role such as the gender role in role congruity theory, where prejudice can arise from failing to meet the prescriptions of a social role over and above the functional role itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Eagly & Karau, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, negative reactions may stem not only from failing to meet leader-, partner-, or follower-role prescriptions but also from not fulfilling the norms of being a "good robot" or "trustworthy algorithm."

Empirical evidence illustrates this dynamic: agents that make mistakes (Dietvorst et al., 2015; Weidemann & Russwinkel, 2021), act unpredictably (Salem et al., 2013), cheat (Herath et al., 2018), or display humanlike affect or behavior such as anger (Herdel et al., 2024), dialect (Kühne et al., 2023), or humming (Liu et al., 2023) violate this artificial agent schema.
text.formatted: Empirical evidence illustrates this dynamic: agents that make mistakes <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Dietvorst et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b134">Weidemann & Russwinkel, 2021)</ref>, act unpredictably <ref type="bibr" target="#b118">(Salem et al., 2013)</ref>, cheat <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Herath et al., 2018)</ref>, or display humanlike affect or behavior such as anger <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Herdel et al., 2024)</ref>, dialect <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Kühne et al., 2023)</ref>, or humming <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">(Liu et al., 2023)</ref> violate this artificial agent schema.

text.text: Such violations can lead observers to downgrade agents to malfunctioning tools or react with abjection (Banks et al., 2023; Einola & Khoreva, 2023), while in other cases they "upgrade" agents to social actors due to an increase in mind perception (as this behavior is more humanlike).
text.formatted: Such violations can lead observers to downgrade agents to malfunctioning tools or react with abjection <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Banks et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Einola & Khoreva, 2023)</ref>, while in other cases they "upgrade" agents to social actors due to an increase in mind perception (as this behavior is more humanlike).

text.text: Integrating this artificial agent schema into the AARC model adds a second dimension of role incongruity in artificial agent evaluation, arising not only from mismatched organizational roles but also from deviations from the normative expectations embedded in the artificial agent role itself.

The reviewed evidence also points to a contingency that the model does not yet formalize: the context in which a role is embedded shapes how strongly its prescriptions emphasize the task versus the social-emotional dimension.
The composition of our database illustrates this.

For agents in follower roles, evidence is concentrated in service and caregiving settings (23 of 37 studies, 62%), where role prescriptions emphasize warmth and responsiveness; the congruity we observe is therefore most directly a statement about service contexts.

Leader-role evidence comes predominantly from internal employee and management settings (10 of 17 studies, 59%), where moral and relational prescriptions are most demanding, which sharpens the incongruity we observe.

We propose that artificial agents will be evaluated as less incongruent in leader roles whose context emphasizes task prescriptions over social-emotional ones, such as data-intensive allocation or monitoring tasks, and as more incongruent in follower or partner roles whose context elevates social-emotional prescriptions, such as care work.
We therefore treat the generalizability of our role-specific conclusions accordingly (see the scope and boundary conditions in the Online Supplement, Section A).
Our findings translate into concrete guidance for managers deploying artificial agents and for designers building them (Chhillar & Aguilera, 2022; Kellogg et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Our findings translate into concrete guidance for managers deploying artificial agents and for designers building them <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Chhillar & Aguilera, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Kellogg et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: For managers, three priorities stand out.

First, retain human moral oversight in algorithmic management: hybrid human-in-the-loop arrangements increase trust and perceived fairness compared to full automation (De Cremer & McGuire, 2022; Kares et al., 2023).
text.formatted: First, retain human moral oversight in algorithmic management: hybrid human-in-the-loop arrangements increase trust and perceived fairness compared to full automation <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(De Cremer & McGuire, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Kares et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Second, configure leadership as augmentation rather than replacement: combining algorithmic capabilities with human judgment addresses the moral and relational deficits that design alone cannot repair (Raisch & Fomina, 2025; Raisch & Krakowski, 2021).
text.formatted: Second, configure leadership as augmentation rather than replacement: combining algorithmic capabilities with human judgment addresses the moral and relational deficits that design alone cannot repair <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">(Raisch & Fomina, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b110">Raisch & Krakowski, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Field evidence shows that the governance of such arrangements can be configured so that organizations and workers benefit jointly (Kellogg, 2022).
text.formatted: Field evidence shows that the governance of such arrangements can be configured so that organizations and workers benefit jointly <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Kellogg, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Third, specify the role frame explicitly when introducing an agent: role ambiguity produces unmet "colleague" expectations and disappointment, whereas clear framing aligns observer expectations with what the agent can deliver (Einola et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Third, specify the role frame explicitly when introducing an agent: role ambiguity produces unmet "colleague" expectations and disappointment, whereas clear framing aligns observer expectations with what the agent can deliver <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Einola et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: For designers, three principles follow.

First, do not assume that anthropomorphizing agents intended for leader roles will resolve perceived moral deficits: humanlike cues may amplify rather than reduce role incongruity (McGuire & De Cremer, 2023; Yam et al., 2022).
text.formatted: First, do not assume that anthropomorphizing agents intended for leader roles will resolve perceived moral deficits: humanlike cues may amplify rather than reduce role incongruity <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">(McGuire & De Cremer, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b145">Yam et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Second, design for social presence rather than human likeness: responsiveness, relational language, and transparent identity framing build acceptance without uncanny-valley risks.
Third, match design cues to the role: human likeness is well received in follower roles, accepted conditionally in partner roles, and rarely fitting in leader roles.
These principles rest on convergent evidence: social presence matters more for acceptance and cooperation than humanlike appearance (Elshan et al., 2022).
text.formatted: These principles rest on convergent evidence: social presence matters more for acceptance and cooperation than humanlike appearance <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Elshan et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Presence cues such as relational language, immediacy, and transparent identity framing raise trust and willingness to rely on the system.
Humanlike appearance alone, however, may be insufficient to support social presence in human-AI collaboration (Siemon et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Humanlike appearance alone, however, may be insufficient to support social presence in human-AI collaboration <ref type="bibr" target="#b122">(Siemon et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Strong cues can also backfire: excessive perceived autonomy reduces cooperation through a reactance process of "agency-cued abjection," a feeling of unease and rejection (Banks et al., 2023), and reading an agent's outputs as signs of "reasoning" encourages false confidence in its capability (Kambhampati et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Strong cues can also backfire: excessive perceived autonomy reduces cooperation through a reactance process of "agency-cued abjection," a feeling of unease and rejection <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Banks et al., 2023)</ref>, and reading an agent's outputs as signs of "reasoning" encourages false confidence in its capability <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Kambhampati et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: More broadly, these prescriptions show what human-centric deployment of artificial agents requires in practice: respecting the role expectations through which workers grant legitimacy to a technology, so that efficiency gains do not come at the cost of the warmth, morality, and fairness that make any role occupant acceptable.
Our review has limitations.
First, the database covers peer-reviewed journal articles, so cutting-edge findings from conference proceedings in cognate fields such as computer science and human-robot interaction may be missing.
Future reviews could broaden the inclusion criteria to high-quality conference proceedings to mitigate this.
Second, the final coding scheme was applied by the lead author after a two-phase scheme development.

Although the procedure is described in the Method, the inter-coder checks are documented in the Online Supplement, and the full coding is openly available, single-coder application remains a constraint.
Third, the evidence base is unevenly distributed across contexts: follower-role evidence concentrates in service and caregiving settings and leader-role evidence in internal organizational settings.
This calls for further investigations into the generalizability of role-specific conclusions (see the scope and boundary conditions in the Online Supplement, Section A).
Building on the AARC model and our review findings, we outline opportunities in three areas: theory development, measurement and design, and organizational consequences.
Table 3 provides an overview of these opportunities, which we elaborate in the following subsections.
