text.text: Role theory distinguishes a structural-functional view, in which roles are relatively fixed positions with prescriptive expectations, and a symbolic-interactionist view, in which roles are negotiated in interactions (Anglin et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Role theory distinguishes a structural-functional view, in which roles are relatively fixed positions with prescriptive expectations, and a symbolic-interactionist view, in which roles are negotiated in interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Anglin et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In the reviewed research, evaluations of artificial agents in leader roles typically follow the structural-functional logic of role congruity theory (del Carmen Triana et al., 2024; Eagly & Karau, 2002): Agents are formally introduced as supervisors or managers, and observers compare prescribed leader expectations with attributes ascribed from design-based cues to judge role congruity or role incongruity.
text.formatted: In the reviewed research, evaluations of artificial agents in leader roles typically follow the structural-functional logic of role congruity theory <ref type="bibr">(del Carmen Triana et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Eagly & Karau, 2002)</ref>: Agents are formally introduced as supervisors or managers, and observers compare prescribed leader expectations with attributes ascribed from design-based cues to judge role congruity or role incongruity.

text.text: In contrast, studies of artificial agents in partner and follower roles often report patterns that we interpret as role ambiguity or role conflict.

We derive this from evidence that participants waver between different role labels and expectations, or explicitly question what the agent "really is," for example when an algorithm formally introduced as a "colleague" was later described by employees as a "shiny tool" when partner role expectations were not met (Einola et al., 2024).
text.formatted: We derive this from evidence that participants waver between different role labels and expectations, or explicitly question what the agent "really is," for example when an algorithm formally introduced as a "colleague" was later described by employees as a "shiny tool" when partner role expectations were not met <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Einola et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Likewise, platform algorithms that fulfill toollike functions (e.g., navigation) and supervisory functions (e.g., giving directives and enforcing performance ratings) blur tool, follower, and leader categories and evoke competing role expectations (Tarafdar et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Likewise, platform algorithms that fulfill toollike functions (e.g., navigation) and supervisory functions (e.g., giving directives and enforcing performance ratings) blur tool, follower, and leader categories and evoke competing role expectations <ref type="bibr" target="#b128">(Tarafdar et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: We encourage future research to clarify when evaluations are primarily driven by structural-functional role prescriptions and when they are shaped by negotiated role meanings, and to specify boundary conditions under which role incongruity, role ambiguity, or role conflict best captures responses to artificial agents.

Such clarification matters because role prescriptions themselves may shift: some argue that artificial agents could come to address followers' basic psychological needs better than human leaders (Van Quaquebeke & Gerpott, 2023), which would make the leader-role deficits we document contingent rather than constant.
text.formatted: Such clarification matters because role prescriptions themselves may shift: some argue that artificial agents could come to address followers' basic psychological needs better than human leaders <ref type="bibr" target="#b131">(Van Quaquebeke & Gerpott, 2023)</ref>, which would make the leader-role deficits we document contingent rather than constant.

text.text: While role (in)congruity represents the primary evaluative mechanism in the AARC model, alternative pathways may also explain resistance toward artificial agents.
One such pathway is status incongruity, which occurs when an agent's assigned hierarchical position conflicts with established social norms and expectations (Rudman et al., 2012).
text.formatted: One such pathway is status incongruity, which occurs when an agent's assigned hierarchical position conflicts with established social norms and expectations <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">(Rudman et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Leader roles imply higher status and influence, whereas artificial agents are typically viewed as technologies that support or accompany human workers (Lee & See, 2004).
text.formatted: Leader roles imply higher status and influence, whereas artificial agents are typically viewed as technologies that support or accompany human workers <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Lee & See, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: When this hierarchy is reversed, such as when an artificial agent leads or evaluates human employees, observers may perceive the hierarchy as inappropriate and question the agent's legitimacy (e.g., Jeon, 2022).
text.formatted: When this hierarchy is reversed, such as when an artificial agent leads or evaluates human employees, observers may perceive the hierarchy as inappropriate and question the agent's legitimacy (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Jeon, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, algorithmic management can reduce perceptions of job complexity and status of human organizational members, reinforcing this incongruity between human subordinates and machine supervisors (e.g., Jago et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Similarly, algorithmic management can reduce perceptions of job complexity and status of human organizational members, reinforcing this incongruity between human subordinates and machine supervisors (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Jago et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Future research could examine how mind-role and status incongruities jointly influence acceptance across hierarchical contexts.
There are still almost no direct tests of role (in)congruity or systematic baselines for specific agent designs, with only a few notable exceptions.

Some recent studies begin to operationalize role (in)congruity or mind-role (mis)fit by measuring both role requirements and perceived agent characteristics, showing that mismatches between the two can shape perceptions and reactions to artificial agents (Dong et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Some recent studies begin to operationalize role (in)congruity or mind-role (mis)fit by measuring both role requirements and perceived agent characteristics, showing that mismatches between the two can shape perceptions and reactions to artificial agents <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Dong et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Further, evidence establishing causality for role incongruity as the underlying mechanism remains limited; one exception is experimental work that manipulates mind perception, agency and experience, to test their direct impact on behavior and moral judgment (Lanz et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Further, evidence establishing causality for role incongruity as the underlying mechanism remains limited; one exception is experimental work that manipulates mind perception, agency and experience, to test their direct impact on behavior and moral judgment <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(Lanz et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These early efforts are promising but underscore the need for more empirically rigorous evidence linking mind-role fit to target evaluations and outcomes.

In addition, methods such as polynomial regression and response-surface analysis (Tsai, Kim, et al., 2022) could provide a formal approach to testing AARC's proposed mechanisms by explicitly measuring how both role prescriptions and design cues jointly predict perceived fit, enabling direct tests of the "roles > design" and "design > roles" patterns identified in this review.
text.formatted: In addition, methods such as polynomial regression and response-surface analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b129">(Tsai, Kim, et al., 2022)</ref> could provide a formal approach to testing AARC's proposed mechanisms by explicitly measuring how both role prescriptions and design cues jointly predict perceived fit, enabling direct tests of the "roles > design" and "design > roles" patterns identified in this review.

text.text: Organizational case studies reveal mixed reactions, with negative evaluations of artificial agents coexisting with optimism about their future capabilities or positive implications for employees' work meaningfulness (e.g., Einola et al., 2024; Goštautaitė et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Organizational case studies reveal mixed reactions, with negative evaluations of artificial agents coexisting with optimism about their future capabilities or positive implications for employees' work meaningfulness (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Einola et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Goštautaitė et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Scenario-based vignette studies may yield more negative responses, potentially because participants imagine rather than experience the interaction (e.g., Liao et al., 2024; Savela et al., 2021), whereas field experiments that combine real task engagement with experimental control suggest that human-agent differences may diminish under real behavioral conditions (Dong et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Scenario-based vignette studies may yield more negative responses, potentially because participants imagine rather than experience the interaction (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Liao et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b119">Savela et al., 2021)</ref>, whereas field experiments that combine real task engagement with experimental control suggest that human-agent differences may diminish under real behavioral conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Dong et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Research design may therefore function as a boundary condition: direct and sustained interaction may allow initial evaluations to become more differentiated as people gain experience with an artificial agent.

Future work should move beyond short vignettes, "Wizard of Oz" experiments (where a hidden human controls the system), and other brief simulations toward designs built on real rather than hypothetical interaction.

Even simple, well-controlled lab studies with genuine agent interaction would help, and longitudinal and field designs could track how trust, legitimacy, and cooperation develop over time in real workplaces.
Baseline Comparisons as Benchmark.

Most research on artificial agents relies on relative comparisons such as human versus agent leaders or high versus low anthropomorphism, without including a baseline in which participants perform the task without guidance from either a human or an artificial agent.
Although informative, such designs make it hard to see whether differences reflect genuine role-design effects or artifacts of the comparison.
Evidence from our review underscores this concern.

In experiments that included a self-directed or "passive" baseline, both human and robot guidance reduced perceived control relative to freely chosen actions, indicating that the loss of agency stemmed from being instructed rather than from the agent's identity (Barlas, 2019).
text.formatted: In experiments that included a self-directed or "passive" baseline, both human and robot guidance reduced perceived control relative to freely chosen actions, indicating that the loss of agency stemmed from being instructed rather than from the agent's identity <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Barlas, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: These findings align with recent methodological critiques that comparisons between two active conditions can produce pseudo effects that may obscure underlying mechanisms (e.g., Stark et al., 2026).
text.formatted: These findings align with recent methodological critiques that comparisons between two active conditions can produce pseudo effects that may obscure underlying mechanisms (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b124">Stark et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Future research should therefore additionally incorporate no-treatment baselines, where appropriate, alongside comparisons with a human leader performing the same task.

Recent reviews of human-agent teams show that mixed teams frequently cause in-group versus out-group categorization processes, with artificial agents often treated as out-group members (Bezrukova et al., 2023; Wolf & Stock-Homburg, 2023).
text.formatted: Recent reviews of human-agent teams show that mixed teams frequently cause in-group versus out-group categorization processes, with artificial agents often treated as out-group members <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Bezrukova et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b140">Wolf & Stock-Homburg, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Examples from our review mirror this pattern: introducing robot teammates reduces identification and psychological attachment, particularly as the number of robot teammates increases (Savela et al., 2021), whereas collaboration improves when at least one additional human partner is present (e.g., Georganta & Ulfert, 2024; Musick et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Examples from our review mirror this pattern: introducing robot teammates reduces identification and psychological attachment, particularly as the number of robot teammates increases <ref type="bibr" target="#b119">(Savela et al., 2021)</ref>, whereas collaboration improves when at least one additional human partner is present (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Georganta & Ulfert, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">Musick et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: These out-group effects are conceptually distinct from, but consequential for, role (in)congruity of artificial agents as teammates.

We therefore propose treating in-group versus out-group categorization as a boundary condition in our AARC model: out-group assignment may lower warmth ascriptions and moral expectations, or shift thresholds for judging fit, potentially overshadowing or amplifying role (in)congruity evaluations.
Future research should jointly assess categorization and role-fit processes to clarify when responses to artificial teammates reflect out-group bias, role incongruity, or their combined influence.

Role incongruity of artificial agents in leader roles stems from recognition-based processes (e.g., Lord et al., 2020), where observers rely on design-based cues about who appears to "fit" a leader role.
text.formatted: Role incongruity of artificial agents in leader roles stems from recognition-based processes (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">Lord et al., 2020)</ref>, where observers rely on design-based cues about who appears to "fit" a leader role.

text.text: Yet, potential perceptual biases raise a critical question: can demonstrated performance override these (possibly biased) perceptions?
Early evidence suggests that algorithmic and AI-assisted managers can, in some contexts, perform effectively enough to challenge the biased judgments.
For example, field studies show that algorithmic supervision can improve service quality and customer satisfaction, even if such gains come with trade-offs in efficiency (Gu et al., 2025).
text.formatted: For example, field studies show that algorithmic supervision can improve service quality and customer satisfaction, even if such gains come with trade-offs in efficiency <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Gu et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Large-scale experiments on human-AI collaboration similarly indicate that mixed human-AI teams achieve higher productivity and, in some domains, produce superior output quality relative to human-only teams (Ju & Aral, 2025).
text.formatted: Large-scale experiments on human-AI collaboration similarly indicate that mixed human-AI teams achieve higher productivity and, in some domains, produce superior output quality relative to human-only teams <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Ju & Aral, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These patterns imply that evidence about an agent's actual performance can shift social perception from a recognition-based process, which relies on whether the agent "looks like" a leader, to an inference-based process that places more weight on what the agent demonstrably achieves (Lord et al., 2020).
text.formatted: These patterns imply that evidence about an agent's actual performance can shift social perception from a recognition-based process, which relies on whether the agent "looks like" a leader, to an inference-based process that places more weight on what the agent demonstrably achieves <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">(Lord et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Artificial agents may reshape how third parties perceive the humans who work with or under them.
Early evidence suggests that being managed by an algorithm can change how employees are evaluated by others (Schweitzer & De Cremer, 2024).
text.formatted: Early evidence suggests that being managed by an algorithm can change how employees are evaluated by others <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">(Schweitzer & De Cremer, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Recent evidence extends this pattern along the model's two dimensions: algorithmic management was associated with lower coworkers' affective (warm) trust in newcomers and higher cognitive (task-related) trust (Lin et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Recent evidence extends this pattern along the model's two dimensions: algorithmic management was associated with lower coworkers' affective (warm) trust in newcomers and higher cognitive (task-related) trust <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">(Lin et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Such spillover effects on coworkers, applicants, and external observers were rarely measured in the reviewed studies and represent an organizational-level consequence of role (in)congruity that merits systematic attention.

Our findings suggest that role incongruity for artificial agents acting as leaders is unlikely to be eliminated; it may instead reflect a deeper tension between automation and augmentation (Raisch & Krakowski, 2021).
text.formatted: Our findings suggest that role incongruity for artificial agents acting as leaders is unlikely to be eliminated; it may instead reflect a deeper tension between automation and augmentation <ref type="bibr" target="#b110">(Raisch & Krakowski, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The more decision-making is automated, the greater the need for human oversight and interpretive leadership, so attempts to replace human leaders may increase the demand for distinctly human capabilities such as contextual judgment and social sensemaking.

As we note in the practical implications, the remedy lies less in resolving incongruity through design or framing than in reconfiguring leadership into hybrid forms that combine algorithmic input with human judgment (Raisch & Fomina, 2025).
text.formatted: As we note in the practical implications, the remedy lies less in resolving incongruity through design or framing than in reconfiguring leadership into hybrid forms that combine algorithmic input with human judgment <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">(Raisch & Fomina, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Future research should examine how such hybrid architectures can balance analytical augmentation with human interpretive oversight to manage, rather than eliminate, the persistent role incongruity for nonhuman leaders.

Across organizational roles, artificial agents are evaluated very differently: those in leader roles face persistent incongruity, judged competent but short on the morality and legitimacy that leadership demands; those in follower roles show consistent congruity when their design signals responsiveness and reliability; and those in partner or teammate roles fall in between, with congruity conditional on context and design.

Our Artificial Agent Role Congruity (AARC) model accounts for this variation: evaluations turn on the (in)congruity between role-based prescriptions and the attributes inferred from design-based cues along the task and socialemotional dimensions of social perception.
By extending role congruity theory to nonhuman actors, AARC clarifies when artificial agents are judged as legitimate role occupants and where misfit biases evaluations and outcomes.

This conceptual background motivates the overarching research question that guides our integrative review: How do role-based expectations and design-based inferences fit together for artificial agents in organizational leader, follower, and partner roles?
